memory_update.text: VRT should remain the primary pure-play candidate for integrated data-center power plus thermal infrastructure; evidence is strong but valuation/pricing checks belong in a later layer.
ETN maps more to power-distribution bottlenecks than liquid cooling; track UPS, busway, PDU, switchgear, and grid-to-chip architecture evidence.
TT became more relevant after the 2026 LiquidStack acquisition; track whether direct-to-chip and immersion cooling become material versus legacy chiller exposure.
NVT is a less obvious but high-fit rack/row supplier due to CDUs, manifolds, controls, and high-density power portfolios linked to AI/HPC and OCP-style standardization.

Other plausible US-listed or US-traded names not included due to the five-candidate limit: MOD, JCI, DELL, HPE, GEV, PWR, AMZN, MSFT, GOOGL, META, and Schneider/Legrand ADRs. MOD and JCI are especially relevant for a follow-up cooling-only pass.

Add VRT as the highest-confidence direct public-market candidate for the data-center thermal and on-site power stack because its disclosures cover integrated power, cooling, liquid-cooling CDUs, heat rejection, controls and lifecycle services.

Add ETN as a high-confidence power-distribution candidate; Q1 2026 order/backlog disclosures cite data-center momentum in Electrical Americas and the Boyd Thermal acquisition adds data-center thermal components.

Add TT as a high-confidence AI thermal-management candidate through Trane and LiquidStack; key evidence is NVIDIA DSX-related reference designs and a commercially available 14 MW GigaModular CDU for Vera Rubin-class deployments.
Add NVT as a component/subsystem candidate for rack, liquid-cooling and power-distribution infrastructure; evidence is strong for technical relevance but revenue exposure still needs quantification.

Add MOD as a less-obvious direct cooling-capacity candidate; evidence includes a $4B long-term capacity agreement for Airedale data-center cooling products, but customer concentration and margin quality require follow-up.

Potential next-pass candidates not included due to the five-name cap: Comfort Systems USA (FIX) for mechanical/electrical installation capacity and technology-sector backlog; Hubbell (HUBB) for electrical components; Johnson Controls (JCI) for chillers/building controls; Schneider Electric ADR for non-US-primary exposure.

The node appears to be shifting from generic data-center square footage toward pre-qualified, repeatable reference architectures combining liquid cooling, power distribution, controls, battery/UPS/grid interaction and lifecycle services.
Add NVT as a direct rack-level liquid-cooling and power-distribution candidate; evidence includes NVIDIA GB200-oriented cooling/power products and broader data-center AI deployment portfolio.
Add MOD as a direct data-center thermal-management candidate; $4B Airedale capacity agreement through 2029 materially strengthens chokepoint relevance.
Add POWL as a medium-voltage switchgear and packaged power-system candidate; relevance is strongest if on-site power distribution remains a delay source for AI data centers.
Add BDC as an underappreciated rack/cabinet/connectivity plus partner-enabled cooling integration candidate, especially for retrofit AI capacity.
Add FIX as a deployment-capacity candidate rather than an equipment manufacturer; track MEP labor, modular fabrication, and commissioning as potential bottlenecks.

Need separate pass for ADR/foreign-listed leaders and private suppliers: Schneider Electric, Legrand, Stulz, Delta Electronics, LiquidStack, OptiCool, CoolIT, JetCool, and Motivair may be critical but are not clean US-listed common-stock candidates.
Need validation of market-pricing risk: several candidates may already reflect AI data-center enthusiasm; this layer only expands the universe and does not rank expected returns.

node: Data-center thermal management and on-site power distribution stack
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded universe focuses on US-listed companies with direct product or platform exposure to AI data-center thermal management and on-site power distribution. The highest-fit candidates are integrated power/cooling vendors, high-density electrical distribution suppliers, full thermal-chain HVAC/liquid-cooling providers, and rack-scale AI infrastructure integrators. This is a research universe only, not a buy/sell list. Layer 1B expansion found five US-listed candidates with direct or adjacent exposure to the AI data-center thermal and on-site power stack: Vertiv as the broadest integrated power/cooling platform, Eaton as the electrical power-distribution and newly expanded thermal-components platform, Trane Technologies as a high-capacity liquid-cooling and chiller/thermal-reference-design supplier, nVent as a rack/liquid-cooling/power-distribution component supplier embedded in NVIDIA DSX-related reference architecture, and Modine as a less-obvious but increasingly direct data-center cooling capacity supplier through Airedale. The chokepoint logic is strongest where companies show AI-specific liquid cooling, CDU, rack-density, power-distribution, backlog/order, or reserved-capacity evidence rather than generic HVAC or construction exposure. Expanded the universe around the hypothesis that AI data-center bottlenecks are shifting toward qualified, integrated cooling, rack-level power, switchgear, and deployment capacity.
